In the interests of transparency, eLife publishes the most substantive revision requests and the accompanying author responses.

Acceptance summary:

The driving forces behind the formation of membrane-less organelles within cells have been of significant interest. The results of this article suggest that non-specific electrostatic interactions primarily control phase separation of RNA/protein condensation in a cytoplasmic-like environment. The results suggest that phase separation occurs readily in simulations, and the simulations reproduce experimental results of binary mixtures of proteins and RNA. The predictions made by a theory developed by the authors to explain the experimental results are in good agreement with the simulation data. The combination of the different techniques is commendable, and it is anticipated that the results presented will stimulate additional studies.

Decision letter after peer review:

Thank you for submitting your article "Charge-Driven Phase Condensation of RNA and Proteins Suggests Broad Role of Phase Separation in Cytoplasmic Environments" for consideration by eLife. Your article has been reviewed by three peer reviewers, including Donald Hamelberg as the Reviewing Editor and Reviewer #1, and the evaluation has been overseen by José Faraldo-Gómez as the Senior Editor

The reviewers have discussed the reviews with one another and the Reviewing Editor has drafted this decision to help you prepare a revised submission.

We would like to draw your attention to changes in our revision policy that we have made in response to COVID-19 (https://elifesciences.org/articles/57162). Specifically, we are asking editors to accept without delay manuscripts, like yours, that they judge can stand as eLife papers without additional data, even if they feel that they would make the manuscript stronger. Thus the revisions requested below only address clarity and presentation.

Summary:

The manuscript by Dutagaci et al., describes a combination of coarse-grained (CG) simulations, theory, and experiment to examine the possibility for phase separation to occur in mixed protein-RNA systems that are intended to mimic cytoplasmic conditions. The authors develop a theory to predict and explain experimental results of binary systems. The authors find that phase separation occurs readily in simulations in which cytoplasmic components are modeled as spheres, and they then show that the same simulation models do a reasonable job of reproducing experimental microscopy results obtained for simple binary mixtures of proteins and RNA. Especially encouraging is that good qualitative correspondence is obtained between simulation and experiment with regard to which proteins form condensates with a model small RNA (J345); the predictions made by the theory are also shown to be in quite good agreement with the simulation data. However, it is not completely clear to the reviewers how much the condensates maintain a liquid character. The paper is well written, the results are interesting, and the attempt to combine different techniques is commendable.

The work will be of interest to many in the field. The results would stimulate additional studies and experiments by the authors and others. Below are recommended revisions to improve the manuscript and strengthen the conclusions of the work.

Essential revisions:

1) It is very clear from the beautiful simulation snapshots shown in Figure 1 that phase separation occurs in the CG simulations of the authors' cytoplasm model. There is no question that this is a very interesting and arresting result. What is less convincing, however, is how strong the evidence is in support of the statement that the separated phases seen in the simulations are "liquid condensates". The nice movie provided by the authors gives an impression of two gel phases rather than two liquid phases; gel-like behavior would also seem to be a likely outcome given the absence of hydrodynamic interactions in the simulations. In support of liquid-like behavior, the authors mention that the macromolecular concentrations are consistent with liquid estimates and that, for the tRNA-dominated condensate at least, the RDF has few clear peaks (Figure 1—figure supplement 3); the latter feature, however, could be caused by small displacements of many tRNAs about nearly-fixed positions within the condensates. The authors also argue that their measured translational diffusion coefficients (Dtr) indicate liquid-like behavior. But these are obtained from fits to MSD data with lag times of only up to 20 ns, and it is clear from the plots that the lines are deviating from linearity as the lag time increases up to 50 ns. If the authors were to instead measure Dtr with a series of much longer lag times (e.g. up to 1 us: very feasible given the 1 ms simulation time and the number of molecules in each condensate) then I think that they might find that their Dtr estimates would drop lower and lower as the lag time increases. If so, wouldn't that indicate that the condensates are gels rather than liquids? The phase separation observed by the authors is a sufficiently interesting result to report, without needing to go one step further and say that the observed phases are liquid-like. If the authors really want to argue that the phases they observe are liquid then they need to provide stronger evidence; if not, wouldn't it would be better to just say "phase separation" throughout the manuscript and leave it at that?

2) Related to the point above, the experiments undoubtedly confirm the formation of condensates between RNA and positively charge proteins. However, the nature of the condensates is ambiguous for majority of the RNA/protein systems studied. Surprisingly, it appears that only one of these condensates possibly maintained a liquid character, contrary to simulation results of the multicomponent systems. In general, are two component systems capable of forming liquid phase condensates? What is known?

3) The simulated cytoplasm model is a reduced representation of an atomistic model previously reported by the authors in this journal. The trade-off made here is that the reduced representation allows much longer timescales to be simulated and this may well be the key to the interesting behavior uncovered by the authors. The model itself, however, is very reminiscent of cytoplasm models previously reported in the literature by other groups: starting with seminal work by Bicout and Field, (1996), but continuing with works by Ridgway et al., (2008), McGuffee and Elcock, (2010), Ando and Skolnick, (2010), Qang and Cheung, (2012), Xu et al., (2013), Hasnain etr al., (2014), Trovato and Tozzini, (2014) and probably others. Of these studies, only the Ando and Skolnick paper is cited here. Some of those earlier studies use models *very* similar to that used here, while others employ models that are much more structurally detailed (though not having the explicit solvent used in the authors' previous atomistic MD simulations). While the present study is exciting in both its timescale and its findings, omitting references to those other papers does readers a disservice and makes the authors look ungenerous to others working in the field. A paragraph should be added to the Introduction and Discussion section that cites and acknowledges the good simulation work done by others that came before this study.

4) Given the potential implications for "real life" in vivo, the authors should also provide some deeper discussion of the potential shortcomings of their CG cytoplasm model, e.g. with regard to: (a) components that are only very roughly treated (e.g. the "mRNA" is 6 copies of a 100-nucleotide RNA, which isn't enough to code for anything interesting), (b) components that might be important but that have been left out (DNA? metabolites?), and/or (c) components for which a sphere might not be a particularly good model (see mRNA above).

5) The authors account for bound counterions by modifying the effective charge on each sphere using Equation 5 or Equation 6. It is unclear where these equations came from. Were they made up by the authors (e.g. Equation 6?) or where they obtained from another source?

6) The algorithm used in the simulations should be clarified. As written, it sounds like conventional molecular dynamics (MD) was used, which would be an odd choice since it would mean that the macromolecules would move ballistically between collisions. But in the Materials and methods section we are told that a Langevin thermostat was used in the simulations, which would make them stochastic dynamics (SD) simulations instead.

7) Additional text would be helpful for the legend to Figure 3 and/or Materials and methods section outlining how each of the data points on the phase diagrams in panels A-D were obtained: after multiple readings of this section of the paper it is reasonably clear about where the fit-lines come from, but it is unclear on the much more basic issue of how the actual data points were obtained.

8) In fitting their theory to their simulation data, the authors note that "Mathematically possible solutions include cases where the volume fractions in the cluster exceed what is physically realistic". They therefore restrict their solutions to ones in which the total macromolecular volume is less than 30%. This doesn't seem unreasonable, but the 30% number is somewhat arbitrary. The authors should say how many of their final solutions ended up with a volume of 29.999% as this would tell whether the theory really wanted to settle on a quite different answer than the one ultimately accepted by the authors.

9) It may be worth elaborating on the "… highly ordered arrangement in the RP condensates." It was recently shown that a balance of homotypic and heterotypic interactions might lead to structured condensates (10.1093/nar/gkaa1099).

results.result: Coarse-grained simulations of a bacterial cytoplasm model show spontaneous formation of two types of condensates within 20 µs that remain stable for 1 ms: tRNA-protein condensates and ribosome particle (RP)-protein condensates. The condensates increase in size with system size, consistent with phase separation rather than finite-size cluster formation.
results.evaluation: Claims C31-C49 collectively describe the cytoplasmic simulation setup, condensate formation kinetics, composition, and size-dependent behavior. The findings are internally consistent and supported by multiple analyses including cluster analysis, volume fraction calculations, and size scaling. The interpretation that size scaling indicates phase separation (C43) is reasonable given the observations.

results.result: The tRNA and RP condensates exhibit different physical properties: tRNA condensates have volume fractions (0.42 total, 0.07 tRNA) consistent with liquid phases and smooth radial distributions, while RP condensates have higher volume fractions (0.58 total, 0.26 RP) with distinct peaks suggesting more ordered, gel-like or solid-like phases.
results.evaluation: Claims C50-C57 provide quantitative characterization of condensate properties with specific volume fractions and radial distribution analyses. The interpretation linking volume fractions to phase states is supported by citation to prior literature (C53-C54), and the radial distribution data provides independent confirmation of the different physical states.

results.result: Separate tRNA and RP condensates form due to size differences and differential protein recruitment: tRNA condensates preferentially recruit large proteins (radius ≥3 nm, charge ≥10), while RP condensates recruit smaller proteins (radius ≤3 nm, charge often <10), explained by size-dependent depletion effects and differential electrostatic interactions.
results.evaluation: Claims C58-C64 provide a mechanistic explanation for condensate separation supported by quantitative analysis of protein size and charge distributions (C61-C63) and radial distribution functions showing favorable interactions (C60). The interpretation invokes established theoretical models (Asakura-Oosawa depletion, C58) appropriately.

results.result: Diffusion analysis reveals that tRNA condensates maintain moderate dynamics with diffusion coefficients of 16.3-28.3 nm²/µs inside versus 55.5-59.0 nm²/µs outside condensates, while RP condensates show more restricted diffusion (0.34-0.49 nm²/µs inside vs 0.80 nm²/µs outside), consistent with their more ordered structure.
results.evaluation: Claims C65-C67 and C75-C78 provide quantitative diffusion measurements with error estimates that are internally consistent across cytoplasmic and five-component models. The diffusion data supports the interpretation of different condensate dynamics, though the authors acknowledge limitations of CG simulations for diffusion estimates (C189).

results.result: A simplified five-component model (tRNA, RP, POSL, POSS, CRW) reproduces the key features of cytoplasmic condensation, including separate tRNA and RP condensates forming within 50 µs, with similar cluster size distributions and interaction preferences as the full cytoplasmic model.
results.evaluation: Claims C68-C74 demonstrate that the reduced model captures essential physics of the full system. The consistency between models (C71) and preservation of key interaction patterns (C73) validates the simplification, though minor differences exist (C72). This provides confidence that the mechanism is robust.

results.result: In the five-component model, tRNA condensation requires [POSL]>100 µM, with increasing [RP] raising the critical POSL concentration due to competition for POSL between tRNA and RP. At high [POSL], increasing concentrations lead to larger clusters with lower effective [tRNA] in condensates.
results.evaluation: Claims C79-C89 describe systematic concentration-dependent behavior with mechanistic explanations based on competition for POSL (C81-C84). The findings are supported by multiple supplementary figures showing radial distributions, cluster compositions, and concentration ratios. The crowder effect (C89) provides an important control.

results.result: Temperature-dependent phase diagrams for the five-component model show critical temperatures of 400-535 K with complex behavior: in the absence of ribosomes, increasing [POSL] lowers Tc (reentrant behavior), but with ribosomes present, Tc increases with [POSL], reflecting competition between tRNA and RP for POSL in non-binary mixtures.
results.evaluation: Claims C90-C96 describe phase diagram behavior fitted to established equations (Guggenheim equations). The reentrant behavior without ribosomes (C91-C92) is consistent with binary complex coacervation theory, while the more complex behavior with ribosomes (C93-C95) is appropriately interpreted as reflecting multi-component competition (C96).

results.result: Confocal microscopy experiments with J345 RNA and various proteins show well-defined fluorescent clusters for trypsin, ADH, lysozyme, and LDH, but not for myoglobin or BSA (negative control). RNA-trypsin condensates are relatively small with sizes following an exponential distribution, though imaging is biased toward clusters containing ≥50 RNA molecules due to low labeling fraction (1 in 56).
results.evaluation: Claims C97-C107 describe experimental validation of simulation predictions with appropriate controls (BSA negative control, C100, C102). The authors acknowledge imaging limitations due to labeling fraction (C106-C107), which is important for interpretation. The observation of condensates with predicted proteins but not with myoglobin validates the charge/size requirements.

results.result: RNA-trypsin condensates exhibit liquid-like behavior with droplets merging over ~1 minute, while lysozyme and ADH form more complex morphologies with smaller condensates associating without merging, suggesting less liquid-like character.
results.evaluation: Claims C108-C110 describe differential condensate dynamics supported by time-lapse microscopy (Videos 2-3). The observation of droplet fusion for trypsin (C108) provides direct evidence of liquid behavior, while the different morphologies for other proteins (C109) suggest variation in condensate material properties, though the exact nature remains unclear (C110).

results.result: Dynamic light scattering analysis of RNA-trypsin and RNA-lysozyme samples reveals polydisperse populations with very long correlation times (up to 1 s) attributed to surface adsorption, plus multiple size regimes including ~10 nm oligomers, ~300 nm particles (lysozyme only), and µm-size condensates, qualitatively consistent with microscopy observations.
results.evaluation: Claims C111-C119 describe DLS characterization with appropriate interpretation of polydisperse samples. The multi-exponential fitting approach (C114) is suitable for polydisperse systems. The interpretation of long correlation times as surface adsorption (C113) is reasonable given the absence of visible macroscopic particles. The consistency with microscopy (C119) provides cross-validation.

results.result: Experimental phase diagram mapping for RNA-trypsin shows that phase separation requires minimum protein concentration ([trypsin]≥150 µM at [RNA]=100 µM) and is lost at high RNA concentrations. FRET experiments show increased efficiency from 50 to 150 µM trypsin, with FRET efficiency >0.26 indicating condensates at 100 µM RNA.
results.evaluation: Claims C120-C125 describe systematic experimental mapping of phase boundaries using two independent methods (microscopy and FRET). The establishment of a FRET threshold (C124) provides a quantitative criterion for condensate detection. The interpretation of gradual FRET increase at low protein concentrations as non-condensate clustering (C125) is supported by simulation data.

results.result: Circular dichroism spectroscopy shows that trypsin and J345 RNA retain their folded states upon condensate formation, with the mixture spectrum appearing as a linear combination of individual component spectra without substantial changes in secondary structure.
results.evaluation: Claims C126-C129 describe CD spectroscopy results indicating preservation of protein and RNA structure. The observation that the mixture spectrum is a linear combination (C129) supports the interpretation that no major structural changes occur upon condensation. This is important for validating the assumption that molecules remain folded in condensates.

results.result: NMR spectroscopy shows that characteristic J345 RNA peaks are retained in the presence of proteins but with greatly attenuated intensities (~80% invisible with lysozyme, ~90% with trypsin), interpreted as rotational diffusion retardation due to large condensate size (>100 nm), providing estimates of RNA partitioning between dilute (20% lysozyme, 10% trypsin) and condensed phases but no structural information about RNA in condensates.
results.evaluation: Claims C130-C137 describe NMR characterization with appropriate interpretation of signal attenuation. The retention of peak positions (C132) indicates structural preservation, while intensity loss (C134) is reasonably attributed to slow tumbling of large condensates (C135). The quantitative estimates of phase partitioning (C136) are useful but rely on the assumption that only dilute-phase RNA is visible. The acknowledged limitation (C137) is important.

results.result: Coarse-grained simulations of binary RNA-protein mixtures at κ=0.7 (~20 mM salt) show condensate formation with lysozyme, trypsin, LDH, and ADH, but not with cytochrome C, myoglobin, or BSA, qualitatively matching experimental results. The fraction of RNA in dilute phase is higher with lysozyme (32%) than trypsin (26-27%), in qualitative agreement with NMR estimates.
results.evaluation: Claims C138-C143 describe binary mixture simulations that validate the model against experiments. The qualitative agreement between simulation and experiment for which proteins form condensates (C142) is strong. The comparison with NMR-derived phase partitioning (C143) provides additional validation, though the authors appropriately note that direct quantitative comparison is limited by concentration differences.

results.result: A theoretical model based on Voorn-Overbeek theory with interaction potentials parameterized from atomistic simulations predicts phase separation for a wide range of protein radii and charges. The theory correctly predicts PS for lysozyme, trypsin, LDH, and ADH, and no PS for myoglobin, consistent with experiments and simulations, though it incorrectly predicts PS for cytochrome C.
results.evaluation: Claims C144-C152 describe theoretical model development and validation. The model is appropriately based on established theory (Voorn-Overbeek, C146) with parameterization from atomistic simulations (C147). The use of an alternative charge model (C148) based on better experimental agreement is reasonable. The mostly successful predictions (C150-C151) validate the approach, while the cytochrome C discrepancy (C152) is honestly reported.

results.result: The theoretical model reproduces the concentration-dependent phase diagram for RNA-trypsin in good agreement with experimental data, exhibiting reentrant behavior with minimal and maximal concentrations as expected for complex coacervates. The theory also qualitatively reproduces FRET efficiency trends, predicting gradual increases from growing RNA populations in condensates with increasing protein concentration.
results.evaluation: Claims C153-C157 describe successful quantitative comparison between theory and experiment. The reproduction of the phase diagram (C153) and FRET trends (C156-C157) demonstrates that the theory captures essential physics. The reentrant behavior (C154) is expected for complex coacervates. The limitation regarding solubility (C155) is appropriately noted.

results.result: The study demonstrates that globular macromolecules can condense based on electrostatic complementarity without requiring polymer character or specific binding interactions, suggesting phase separation may be a general phenomenon in cells depending on concentration, charge, and size distributions of nucleic acids and proteins. Cytoplasmic simulations show separate tRNA-protein and ribosome-protein condensates.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C7, C158-C164 summarize the main conclusions supported by the combined simulation, theory, and experimental evidence. The claim that electrostatic complementarity alone is sufficient (C3, C159) is well-supported by the use of globular molecules without specific interactions (C160-C161). The generalization to cellular environments (C162) is appropriately framed as a possibility based on the cytoplasmic simulations (C163).

results.result: The results provide evidence for a general principle of phase separation based on electrostatic complementarity and generalized multivalency, where isotropic spheres are maximally multivalent and globular proteins with distributed positive charges act as polyvalent particles. Size and charge are essential determinants, with optimal packing requiring larger proteins for smaller RNA and smaller proteins for larger ribosomal particles.
results.evaluation: Claims C170-C178 provide mechanistic interpretation of the findings. The concept of generalized multivalency (C171-C173) is well-articulated and supported by the observation that non-specifically interacting globular molecules can phase separate. The size-matching requirement (C177) is directly supported by simulation data showing differential protein recruitment to tRNA vs RP condensates.

results.result: Protein concentration is a critical determinant for phase separation, with simulations and theory predicting minimum concentrations around 0.05 mM or more depending on protein charge and size, validated experimentally for trypsin. Heterogeneous mixtures of similar-sized and charged proteins can promote PS equally well as individual proteins. RNA concentration is less critical at the lower end, though higher RNA concentrations allow larger condensates until a critical concentration is exceeded.
results.evaluation: Claims C179-C185 describe concentration dependencies supported by systematic studies in simulations, theory, and experiments. The experimental validation for trypsin (C181) supports the predicted minimum protein concentration (C180). The finding that heterogeneous protein mixtures work equally well (C182) is important for biological relevance. The competition effects in cytoplasmic models (C185) add complexity relevant to cellular environments.

results.result: The condensates show varying degrees of dynamics: simulations suggest significant dynamics based on diffusion rates (though with acknowledged limitations of CG simulations lacking hydrodynamic interactions), experiments show liquid-like behavior for RNA-trypsin condensates, and NMR results suggest significant retardation of diffusional dynamics inside condensates.
results.evaluation: Claims C186-C192 describe condensate dynamics with mixed evidence. The simulation-based diffusion estimates (C188) are qualified by acknowledged limitations (C189). Experimental evidence for liquid behavior is clear for trypsin (C190) but unclear for other proteins (C191). The NMR data (C192) suggests retarded dynamics but cannot provide structural information inside condensates. The overall picture of condensate dynamics remains incomplete.

results.result: The CG models, while simplified and lacking features like metabolites, membranes, and molecular shape details, enable exploration of large spatial and temporal scales relevant to phase separation. The models are parameterized from atomistic simulations and could be improved with patchy particles or residue-based coarse-graining, though at higher computational cost. Future studies should include missing cellular components and atomistic simulations of clusters.
results.evaluation: Claims C193-C202 provide balanced discussion of model advantages and limitations. The acknowledgment of simplifications (C195, C198-C200) is appropriate, as is the discussion of possible improvements (C196-C197) and future directions (C201-C202). The parameterization from atomistic simulations (C194) provides some validation of the approach.

results.result: The study reports phase separation of RNA and proteins based on charge complementarity, supported by coarse-grained simulations, theory, and experimental validation via multiple techniques. Condensate formation depends on protein concentration, size, and charge. The broader implication is that charge-driven phase separation may be widespread in biology without requiring disordered proteins or RNA, potentially leading to extensive phase separation in cellular cytoplasms with functional consequences such as enhanced translation rates.
results.evaluation: Claims C203-C213 provide concluding summary and broader implications. The main conclusions (C205-C208) are well-supported by the evidence presented. The broader implications about widespread phase separation (C210-C211) are appropriately framed as possibilities requiring further investigation (C213). The speculation about functional consequences (C212) is reasonable but clearly identified as speculation. The acknowledged need for in vivo validation (C204, C213) is appropriate.

results.result: The introduction establishes that phase separation is increasingly recognized as important in cellular organization, with membrane-less organelles forming via coacervation in nucleus and cytoplasm. Well-established drivers include multivalency, intrinsic disorder, and electrostatic interactions, with RNA playing a prominent role. However, it remains unclear what components can lead to condensation in heterogeneous cellular environments.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C30 provide literature context supported by extensive citations. These claims establish the state of the field and identify the knowledge gap (C30) that the study addresses. The characterization of prior work appears accurate based on the citations provided.

results.result: While electrostatic interactions in phase separation are well-established for various molecules, almost all LLPS studies to date involve polymers and IDPs. Examples of PS with folded proteins exist but are generally ascribed to specific multivalent interactions, with evidence for generic electrostatic-only mechanisms only beginning to emerge.
results.evaluation: Claims C165-C169 characterize the existing literature and position the current work. The characterization appears accurate based on the citations provided and appropriately identifies the novelty of the current study in demonstrating electrostatic-only mechanisms without requiring disorder or specific interactions.

results.result: The study employs a multiscale approach combining coarse-grained simulations of a bacterial cytoplasm (parameterized against atomistic MD), reduced five- and two-component models, analytical theory, and experimental validation via confocal microscopy, FRET, NMR spectroscopy, and dynamic light scattering to characterize phase separation and condensate properties.
results.evaluation: Claims C4-C6 and C31-C37 describe the comprehensive methodological approach. The combination of multiple computational and experimental methods provides strong validation through orthogonal approaches. The parameterization of CG models against atomistic simulations (C32) provides a physical basis for the simplified models.
